slides.title: Day 1 · The map
slides.body:
Two-thirds of US electricity is used in regions where an independent operator runs the grid and its market. FERC counts seven regional operators: CAISO in California, MISO in the Midcontinent, ISO New England, NYISO in New York, PJM in the Mid-Atlantic and Midwest, SPP in the Southwest, and ERCOT in Texas. Two-thirds of the nation's electricity load is served in their regions.

They run the high-voltage grid independently of the companies that sell power, and they operate bid-based markets that decide which power plants run.

slides.title: Generate, transmit, distribute
slides.body: Power plants generate electricity. High-voltage lines carry it long distances, then distribution lines bring it to customers.

slides.title: The constant job
slides.body: On the grid, supply must constantly match demand. Balancing authorities manage that, region by region.

slides.title: The operators
slides.body: ISOs and RTOs run the high-voltage grid and its markets, and choose which plants run. There are seven in the US, including PJM, MISO and ERCOT.

slides.title: Three grids
slides.body: The US has three big grids: Eastern, Western and Texas. ERCOT runs the grid covering most of Texas.

slides.title: Name the operator
slides.body: Know which ISO or RTO runs the region a company works in. Each has its own market rules and its own challenges.

slides.title: The rule
slides.body: Electricity is made the instant it is used, so someone must run the grid every second.

exercises.kicker: Names like PJM, MISO and ERCOT run the show.
